newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Dta Euro-Asian bond makes mark.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Dta Euro-Asian bond makes mark.

text.p: German bank Deutsche Ausgleichsbank (DtA) sold almost half of a debut Euro-Asian bond to Asian investors on Thursday.

The 1.5 billion mark issue for the AAA-rated borrower was announced in London on Wednesday but launched in early Asian trade Thursday to give the region's investors a chance to buy the bond before European investors came in.
The syndicate also was formed during Asian hours and allotments made, noted Mark Bucknall, head of syndication and debt origination at HSBC Markets in Hong Kong.
"That makes Asian investors happy because they feel they are getting the first crack at the whip rather than the second crack at the whip following Europe's demand," he said.
Just under 50 percent of the bond was placed in Asia, he said.
HSBC Trinkhaus and Commerzbank were joint lead managers and bookrunners.

The bond matures in July 4, 2007. It was priced during European hours to yield 14 basis points over the new six percent German bund due July 4, 2007, toward the tight end of the 14-16 basis points indicated range.
The bond was DtA's first jumbo bond launched into international markets in addition to its first Euro-Asian.
It will be listed in Hong Kong, Singapore, Dusseldorf and Frankfurt. Asian roadshows were held in Tokyo, Beijing, Hong Kong and Singapore.
The bank is a development agency of the German federal goverment that provides funding on favorable conditions to small and medium-sized companies.
HSBC's Bucknall said that until now, Asian investors had accounted for 15-17 percent of Dta's investor base, a figure Dta had hoped to raise to 25 percent this year.

"Hopefully over time and throughout their funding plans for the rest of the year, the success of this transaction will pay off and DtA may finish the year averaging out at 35 percent to Asian investors," said Bucknall.
In Asia, central banks and large investment funds were the biggest takers on the bond, though private banks also showed some interest, Bucknall said.
In other debt news, Hong Kong's Wing Hang Bank launched a HK$1.2 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue.
Chase Manhattan Asia, Schroders Asia, Jardine Fleming Bank and Sakura Finance Asia are the arrangers.
The notes mature in three years and pay an all-in return of 43 basis points to top-tier participants.
Application will be made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Bankers said the Wing Hang deal was most directly comparable to Chekiang First Bank's LAF-eligible FRCD launched last month. Chekiang's three-year paper pays an all-in of 42 basis points.
Most bankers said that Chekiang had a slight edge over Wing Hang because of its higher rating -- Chekiang rates an A-plus from IBCA while Wing Hang is assessed at A-minus.

Chekiang, which is wholly owned by Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, also has stronger parentage, the bankers said. Bank of New York, which had held 30 percent of Wing Hang Bank, last month sold a five percent stake to Singapore Technologies.
Standard and Poor's Corp today assigned an A-plus rating to SK Telecom's US$230 million Yankee bond, which is expected to launch this week via Merrill Lynch.
Elsewhere, the co-chairman of Vietnam's Bank Advisory Committee today said that the country is on target to issue Brady bonds by end-June as part of its debt restructuring plan.

"Everything is on schedule for basically the end of June at this stage," said Rollo Prendergast, committee co-chairman and regional head for Global Structured Finance at ANZ Banking Group in Hong Kong.
